intro: A fencing mask in a museum case, a black cotton belt with a name stitched on it, a berimbau from Salvador, a banzuke printed for a sumo tournament in Tokyo and a copy of the Queensberry Rules of 1867 can all sit on the same table. Each one was made by people for a job. Each one also became evidence. Historians read these objects the way they read letters and laws: for who made them, when, where, and why they were kept.

Objects and papers do not keep themselves. Museums, archives, libraries and halls of fame choose what to save, and their choices leave gaps. Governing bodies publish rule books in new editions. Newspapers report events on deadline and sometimes get them wrong. Legends, such as the story linking Bodhidharma to Shaolin, are told beside records that can be dated, such as a stone stele carved in 728.

In this unit you will read objects as primary sources and write captions that say what an object is, where it came from and who made it. Then you will plan your own short research paper on one tradition. You will gather its founding dates, its governing body, its rule book editions and its records of who was admitted when, and you will cite each institution by name.
bigQuestion: How do objects, rule books, charters and newspapers let us tell a martial art's history truthfully, and whose story do they leave out?

write.prompt: Choose one tradition from this unit, such as judo, capoeira, sumo, fencing or boxing. What do its objects and records show about who was let in, and when? Cite two or three dated records by name, such as the Queensberry Rules (1867), the Penal Code of 1890, a banzuke, or the Kodokan's 1926 women's section.
tips: Name each record and give its date and the institution that made it.
Label any legend as a legend and set it beside a dated record.
Say which governing body you mean each time you name a rule.
Mark any fact that only one source gives as uncertain.
Use unit words such as provenance, edition, charter and corroboration.

title: Object and Plan

chapters.title: Objects as Evidence
chapters.bigQuestion: What can a mask, a belt, a musical bow, a ranking sheet and a printed rule book prove about the past, and what can they not prove?

story.title: A Mask Beside a Rule Book
story.kicker: Two objects in one museum case were made for different jobs, yet both are records of how people fenced.
paragraphs: A senior named Lucía walks through the arms and armor rooms of a large art museum on a class trip. Most cases hold swords and suits of steel from Europe and Japan. One small case near the door holds only two things. On the left is a fencing mask with a front of fine wire mesh. On the right is a thin printed book of fencing rules, open to a page of numbered articles.

The mask has a padded collar and a dark, bent mesh that has been pressed by years of use. Its caption gives a place, a rough date and the words "gift of" followed by a family name. The book's caption names the national fencing group that printed it and the year of its edition. Lucía notices that the two captions are written in the same short, careful style.

Her history teacher points to the book. "That page tells you what the officials were supposed to do," she says. "The mask tells you what one fencer actually wore." Then she points to the words "gift of." "Somebody owned that mask before the museum did. Somebody wrote down how it got here."

Lucía copies both captions into her notebook, word for word. She writes a question under them: who made each object, and who decided it was worth keeping? Later she learns that museum staff call that written trail of owners the object's provenance, and that it can matter as much as the object itself.
story.think: What can a worn mask tell a historian that a printed rule book cannot, and what can the rule book tell that the mask cannot?

lessons.title: Things as Primary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: An object made or used at the time is a primary source, and a historian reads it for who made it, who used it and why it survived.
reading: A *primary source* is evidence made at the time a historian is studying. Letters, photographs and newspapers are primary sources. So are objects. A pair of boxing gloves from the 1890s, a judo belt from the 1930s or a printed sumo ranking sheet from the 1800s each came straight out of its own time.

An *artifact* is an object made or shaped by people. Historians ask the same questions of an artifact that they ask of a document. Who made it, and where? What is it made of? Who used it, and for what? Material matters: a mask of hand-bent iron wire points to a workshop, while a mask of stamped steel mesh points to a factory.

A *secondary source* is a later account that explains the past, such as a history book or an encyclopedia article. It often rests on primary sources. A careful researcher uses both. The primary source gives direct evidence, and the secondary source gives context that one object alone cannot supply.

words.d: evidence made at the time being studied, such as a letter, photograph, newspaper or object
an object made or shaped by people and studied for what it shows about the past
a later account that explains the past, often built on primary sources

look.title: Two Pairs of Gloves
look.text: Picture two pairs of boxing gloves in one case. The first pair is thin, with a little padding sewn inside soft leather and laces at the wrist. The second pair is thick and wide, with a factory label stamped inside the cuff and a hook-and-loop strap. The caption says the first pair dates from the 1890s and the second from the 1990s.
look.prompt: List two questions you would ask about each pair to decide who made it and who used it.

check.q: Which of these is a primary source for boxing in the 1890s?
choices: a pair of gloves made and used in the 1890s
check.why: A primary source was made at the time being studied, so gloves from the 1890s count.

check.q: What is an artifact?
choices: a law passed by a legislature
an object made or shaped by people
a later book that explains the past
check.why: An artifact is an object made or shaped by people and studied as evidence.

check.q: How does a secondary source help a researcher who already has an object?
choices: it replaces the object as evidence
it proves the object is real
it gives context that one object alone cannot supply
it tells the museum what to charge
check.why: A secondary source explains the setting, which a single primary source cannot do by itself.

lessons.title: The Caption on the Case
lessons.mainIdea: A museum caption packs the basic facts about an object into a few lines: what it is, who made it, where, when, of what, and how the museum got it.
reading: Museum workers often call the short basic caption beside an object a *tombstone label*, because it is brief and factual like the words carved on a grave marker. It usually names the object, the maker if known, the place and date it was made, and the materials. The date is often given as "c." for circa, meaning about, when the exact year is unknown.

Near the bottom of many captions is a *credit line*. It tells how the object came to the museum, such as "gift of" a person or "purchase" with a named fund. Many captions also print an *accession number*. That number is the museum's own catalog code for the object, often starting with the year it entered the collection.

A good caption does not guess. If the maker is unknown, it says so. If only the country is known, it gives the country and not a city. When a researcher writes a caption, the same rules help: state what the object is, where it came from and who made it, and mark every date that is only an estimate.

words.d: museum term for a short caption giving an object's name, maker, place, date and materials
the part of a caption that says how a museum got an object, such as a gift or a purchase
a museum's catalog code for one object, often beginning with the year it arrived

look.title: A Caption to Check
look.text: Fencing mask. France, c. 1880s. Iron wire mesh, leather, cotton padding. Maker unknown. Gift of a private donor.
look.prompt: Which parts of this caption are certain, and which are estimates? What one fact would you most want to add?

check.q: What does "c. 1880s" on a caption mean?
choices: made at about that time; the exact year is unknown
check.why: The letter c stands for circa, which means about.

check.q: What does a credit line tell you?
choices: how the museum got the object
check.why: A credit line says whether the object was a gift, a purchase or came some other way.

check.q: What should a careful caption say if the maker is not known?
choices: the name of the most famous maker of the time
nothing at all about the object
the name of the donor as the maker
check.why: A good caption does not guess; it states that the maker is unknown.

lessons.title: The Chain of Owners
lessons.mainIdea: Provenance is the recorded history of who owned an object, and museums check it to make sure an object was obtained honestly.
reading: *Provenance* is the history of an object's owners, from the maker to today. Researchers trace it through bills of sale, auction catalogs, letters, old photographs and museum files. A belt with a clear provenance might be traced from the teacher who awarded it, to the student who wore it, to the family who gave it to a museum.

Gaps in provenance raise questions. If an object's owners are unknown for decades, it may have been lost, sold quietly or taken. The International Council of Museums, known as ICOM, was founded in 1946. Its Code of Ethics for Museums, first adopted in 1986 and revised in 2004, asks museums to check that an object was not illegally obtained before they acquire it.

Provenance also affects meaning. A sumo ranking sheet printed for a tournament and kept by a fan tells a different story than one kept by a stable, the training group a wrestler lives in. When a researcher cites an object, naming its *donor* and its known owners lets readers see how the object reached the case.

words.d: the recorded history of who has owned an object, from its maker to today
a person or group who gives an object or money to a museum or archive
the International Council of Museums, founded in 1946, which publishes a code of ethics for museums

look.title: A Museum Ethics Rule
look.text: Before a museum acquires an object, it should make every effort to be sure the object was not illegally obtained in, or illegally exported from, its country of origin or any country where it was owned legally.
look.cite: International Council of Museums, ICOM Code of Ethics for Museums (revised 2004), section on acquiring collections
look.prompt: Why would a museum need to know an object's owners before it accepts the object?

check.q: What is provenance?
choices: the price an object sold for
the material an object is made of
the recorded history of who owned an object
the room where an object is shown
check.why: Provenance is the chain of owners from the maker to today.

check.q: Which group publishes the Code of Ethics for Museums first adopted in 1986?
check.why: ICOM, founded in 1946, adopted its Code of Ethics in 1986 and revised it in 2004.

check.q: Why does a long gap in an object's provenance matter?
choices: the object may have been lost, sold quietly or taken
it proves the object is a fake
it means the object is very valuable
it shows the maker was famous
check.why: A gap raises questions about how the object moved from owner to owner.

sections.title: The Mask and the Rule Book

lessons.title: Wire Mesh in France
lessons.mainIdea: Wire-mesh fencing masks spread in eighteenth-century France, and a surviving mask can show when and where fencing became a supervised practice.
reading: Fencing with blunted swords for training is very old in Europe. Fencing masters in Italy, Spain, France and the German lands published books about it from the 1500s on. For a long time, training bouts were fought with little or no protection for the face, and serious eye injuries were a known danger of the fencing school.

In eighteenth-century France, fencing masters began to use masks with a front of woven wire. Tradition credits the Paris master Nicolas Texier de La Boëssière with popularizing the mesh mask in the mid-1700s, though historians note that similar masks may have existed earlier. By the 1800s, wire *mesh* masks were standard in fencing schools across Europe.

A mask in a museum can show how the practice changed. Early masks used hand-bent iron wire and leather. Later masks added a padded bib to protect the throat. Modern competition masks must pass strength tests set by the *FIE*, the International Fencing Federation, founded in Paris in 1913. The changing mask is a record of rising safety rules.

words.d: a net of woven wire; the see-through front of a fencing mask
Fédération Internationale d'Escrime, the International Fencing Federation, founded in Paris in 1913
a teacher who ran a fencing school and often wrote books about its methods

look.title: Two Masks Compared
look.text: Mask A has a front of uneven iron wire, a narrow leather rim and no throat cover. Mask B has a tight, even steel mesh, a thick padded bib hanging below the chin and a small stamped mark inside the rim.
look.prompt: Which mask is probably older? Which clues in the description support your answer?

check.q: In which country did wire-mesh fencing masks spread in the 1700s?
check.why: Fencing masters in eighteenth-century France popularized the wire-mesh mask.

check.q: When and where was the FIE founded?
check.why: The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913.

check.q: Why do historians call the La Boëssière story a tradition rather than a settled fact?
choices: similar masks may have existed earlier
La Boëssière never lived in Paris
check.why: He is credited by tradition, but earlier mesh masks may have existed, so the credit is not certain.

lessons.title: Wires, Jackets and Lights
lessons.mainIdea: Electric scoring came to Olympic fencing weapon by weapon, in 1936, 1956 and 1988, and the gear that made it possible is a dated record of the change.
reading: Before electric scoring, fencing officials called touches by eye. A president of the jury watched the bout while assistant judges watched each fencer. Arguments over close calls were common. Inventors in Europe worked on electric systems in the early 1900s, in which a touch closed a circuit and lit a lamp or rang a bell.

The FIE brought electric scoring into Olympic fencing one weapon at a time. The épée used it at the 1936 Berlin Games. The foil followed at the 1956 Melbourne Games. The sabre was last, at the 1988 Seoul Games. Each change needed new gear, including a body wire running under the jacket to a reel at the end of the strip.

For foil and sabre, fencers wear a *lamé*, a jacket woven with metal thread that marks the target area for the scoring machine. A lamé in a museum case is evidence of a rule: only touches on the area it covers count. A *scoring box* with colored lights is evidence of a new kind of official, a machine that shares the job with the referee.

words.d: a fencing jacket woven with metal thread that shows the scoring machine where the target is
the electric machine that lights up when a touch is registered in fencing
one of the three fencing weapons, the first to use electric scoring at the Olympics, in 1936

look.title: Electric Scoring at the Olympics
look.unit: year first used at the Olympic Games
look.cite: FIE and IOC Olympic results records, Berlin 1936, Melbourne 1956, Seoul 1988
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first and last weapon to use electric scoring?

check.q: At which Olympic Games was electric scoring first used for the épée?
check.why: Épée was the first weapon to use electric scoring, at Berlin in 1936.

check.q: What does a lamé show the scoring machine?
choices: how long the bout has lasted
which country the fencer is from
check.why: The metal thread in a lamé marks the target area for foil and sabre.

check.q: Which fencing weapon was the last to use electric scoring at the Olympics?
check.why: Sabre adopted electric scoring last, at the 1988 Seoul Games.

lessons.title: Three Boxing Codes
lessons.mainIdea: Printed boxing codes from 1743, 1838 and 1867 are dated primary sources that show how a violent prize fight became a timed, gloved sport.
reading: In 1743 the London boxer and showman Jack Broughton published a short set of rules for bouts at his amphitheater. *Broughton's Rules* set a square marked on the floor and said a fallen man had half a minute to return to it. They also allowed umpires chosen by the two sides. These were among the first written boxing rules in England.

In 1838 a longer code, the *London Prize Ring Rules*, replaced Broughton's. It called for a roped ring of 24 feet square. It was revised in 1853. Under these rules, fighters still used bare fists, and a round ended only when a man went down, so fights could last for hours. Prize fighting was illegal in much of Britain and the United States, and bouts were often held in secret.

In 1867 the *Queensberry Rules* were published in London. They were written by the Welsh sportsman John Graham Chambers and issued under the name of John Sholto Douglas, the ninth Marquess of Queensberry. They required gloves, three-minute rounds with one minute of rest, and a count of ten for a fallen boxer. Each code, read in order, shows rule writers and sporting clubs pushing boxing toward limits.

words.d: boxing rules published by Jack Broughton in London in 1743
a bare-knuckle boxing code of 1838, revised in 1853
the 1867 boxing code written by John Graham Chambers, requiring gloves and timed rounds

look.title: Three Printed Boxing Codes
look.cite: Broughton's Rules (1743); London Prize Ring Rules (1838, rev. 1853); Queensberry Rules (1867)
look.prompt: How many years separate the first code and the Queensberry Rules?

check.q: Who wrote the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: Chambers wrote them; they were issued under the Marquess of Queensberry's name in 1867.

check.q: Which code still used bare fists and rounds that ended only when a man went down?
check.why: The London Prize Ring Rules of 1838 kept bare fists and untimed rounds.

check.q: What year were Broughton's Rules published?
check.why: Jack Broughton published his rules in London in 1743.

lessons.title: Reading One Printed Rule
lessons.mainIdea: A single printed rule, read closely with its date and author, shows what a governing group wanted to change and what it feared.
reading: A printed rule book is an artifact as well as a text. The paper, the printer's name and the edition number are evidence. Copies of the Queensberry Rules were printed in sporting papers and handbooks, so historians can compare versions. A rule book held in a library catalog usually lists its publisher, its city and its year.

The Queensberry Rules did not take over at once. Bare-knuckle fights under the London rules went on for decades. The first world heavyweight title fight widely described as fought under Queensberry rules with gloves came on September 7, 1892, in New Orleans. James J. Corbett defeated John L. Sullivan in the 21st round. Newspapers across the United States reported it.

Reading a rule closely means asking why it was written. A rule setting three-minute rounds limited how long a boxer could fight without rest. A rule requiring gloves separated the new sport from illegal prize fights. A *code* is a full set of rules, and each rule in it answers a problem the writers had seen. A researcher names the *edition* read, because wording can change.

words.d: a complete, written set of rules for a sport or group
one printing of a book; later editions may change the wording
American boxer who won the heavyweight title from John L. Sullivan in New Orleans in 1892

look.title: The Timing Rule
look.text: The rounds are to last three minutes, with one minute's rest between rounds.
look.prompt: What problem from the bare-knuckle era might this rule have been written to solve?

check.q: Who won the 1892 heavyweight title fight in New Orleans?
check.why: Corbett defeated Sullivan in the 21st round on September 7, 1892.

check.q: Why should a researcher name the edition of a rule book?
choices: the wording can change between editions
every edition has the same wording
editions are only used for novels
check.why: Later editions may change rules, so the edition tells readers which wording was used.

check.q: What is a code in sports history?
choices: a complete, written set of rules
check.why: A code is a full set of written rules, like the Queensberry Rules of 1867.

sections.title: The Belt and the Ranking Sheet

lessons.title: What a Belt Records
lessons.mainIdea: A judo belt is a record of a ranking system that Kanō Jigorō began at the Kodokan in the 1880s and that later teachers expanded with colors.
reading: Kanō Jigorō founded the *Kodokan*, his judo school, in 1882 at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. In 1883 he gave the first *dan* ranks to two students, Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō. Dan means step or grade. Kanō borrowed the idea of numbered grades from the board game go, which already ranked players by dan.

By the late 1880s, Kodokan students with dan ranks wore a black sash, or obi, over their practice clothes. Students below dan held *kyu* grades, which count downward toward the first dan. In Japan, kyu students long wore white or a small number of colors. The many-colored belt ladder seen in Western schools came later.

In Paris in the 1930s, the Japanese judo teacher Kawaishi Mikinosuke is widely credited with adding a sequence of colored belts for kyu grades. He believed colors would help European students see their progress. Other arts, including karate and taekwondo, later used colored belts too. A belt in a museum case records a school, a teacher and a moment in this long history.

words.d: the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882, still the world center of judo
a numbered grade meaning step; in judo, the ranks that begin at black belt
a grade below dan, counting downward toward the first dan

look.title: A Belt With a Name
look.text: A worn black cotton belt lies in a case. Stitched in small letters near one end are a person's name and the name of a judo club. The caption gives a city, a decade and the words "gift of the family."
look.prompt: What does the stitching let a researcher look for in other records? Name two places you might search.

check.q: Where did Kanō Jigorō found the Kodokan in 1882?
check.why: The Kodokan began at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo, in 1882.

check.q: From what game did Kanō borrow the idea of dan ranks?
check.why: Go already ranked players by dan, and Kanō adapted the idea for judo in 1883.

check.q: Who is widely credited with adding colored kyu belts in Paris in the 1930s?
check.why: Kawaishi, teaching judo in Paris, is widely credited with the colored belt ladder.

lessons.title: The Banzuke Sheet
lessons.mainIdea: The banzuke is sumo's printed ranking list, written by hand in a special brush style and issued before every tournament.
reading: A *banzuke* is the official ranking list of professional sumo. Printed banzuke were already being sold in Edo, the old name for Tokyo, by the mid-1700s. The sheet lists every wrestler in order of rank, with the highest names in the largest characters at the top. Wrestlers are split into an east side and a west side, and east is treated as slightly higher.

The banzuke is written by hand by senior *gyōji*, the referees of sumo, before it is printed. They use a thick, crowded brush style called sumō-ji. The style is often linked to the Negishi family of printers in Edo. Lower ranks are written in smaller and smaller characters, so the names at the bottom are very hard to read without a lens.

Today the Japan Sumo Association releases the banzuke about two weeks before each tournament. The top division is called makuuchi. Its ranks, from highest, are yokozuna, ōzeki, sekiwake, komusubi and maegashira. A collection of banzuke in order lets a historian trace one wrestler's rise and fall, tournament by tournament, across a whole career.

words.d: the official printed ranking list of professional sumo, issued before each tournament
a sumo referee; senior gyōji also write the banzuke by hand
the highest rank in professional sumo
the top division of professional sumo

look.title: Ranks in the Top Division
look.prompt: Which rank sits just below ōzeki on the banzuke?

check.q: Who writes the banzuke by hand?
check.why: Senior sumo referees, called gyōji, write the banzuke in sumō-ji brush style.

check.q: What is the highest rank in professional sumo?
check.why: Yokozuna is the top rank; maegashira is the lowest rank in makuuchi.

check.q: Why can a set of banzuke in order help a historian?
choices: it traces one wrestler's rank tournament by tournament
check.why: Each sheet records rank at one tournament, so a series shows a career.

lessons.title: Six Tournaments a Year
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1958, professional sumo has held six official tournaments a year in four cities, and each banzuke belongs to one of them.
reading: An official sumo tournament is called a *honbasho*. Since 1958, the Japan Sumo Association has held six honbasho a year. Three are in Tokyo, in January, May and September. The others are in Osaka in March, Nagoya in July and Fukuoka in November. Each lasts fifteen days, and each has its own banzuke.

The Tokyo tournaments are held at the Ryōgoku *Kokugikan*, a hall that opened in 1985 in the Ryōgoku district. The building also houses the Sumo Museum, which keeps banzuke, prints, and other records of the sport's past. Because each sheet has a tournament name and date, a museum can arrange its banzuke like pages in a calendar.

Sumo keeps rules about who may enter the *dohyō*, the raised clay ring. By long custom, women are not allowed to step into it, a rule the Japan Sumo Association links to tradition. In April 2018, women who rushed into a ring in Maizuru to give first aid to a collapsed official were asked over the loudspeaker to leave. The event set off a national debate in Japan.

words.d: an official professional sumo tournament; six are held each year
the sumo hall in Tokyo's Ryōgoku district, opened in its current building in 1985
the raised clay ring in which sumo bouts take place

look.title: A Calendar of Sheets
look.text: A museum drawer holds six banzuke from one year, each labeled with a month and a city: January, Tokyo; March, Osaka; May, Tokyo; July, Nagoya; September, Tokyo; November, Fukuoka.
look.prompt: If one sheet were missing, how could a researcher tell which tournament it belonged to?

check.q: Since what year have six honbasho been held each year?
check.why: The six-tournament calendar began in 1958.

check.q: In which month is the Osaka tournament held?
check.why: Osaka hosts the March honbasho; Nagoya is July and Fukuoka November.

check.q: What happened in Maizuru in April 2018?
choices: women giving first aid were asked to leave the ring
check.why: Women who entered the ring to help a collapsed official were told to leave, starting a national debate.

sections.title: The Musical Bow and the Keepers

lessons.title: The Berimbau
lessons.mainIdea: The berimbau is the musical bow that leads the capoeira roda, and its history links Afro-Brazilian communities to Central African musical bows.
reading: The *berimbau* is a musical bow. It has a wooden bow called the verga, a single steel wire called the arame, and a hollow gourd called the cabaça that makes the sound louder. Musical bows of this kind were played in Central and Southern Africa, including the region of present-day Angola. Enslaved Africans carried the knowledge of such bows to Brazil.

In capoeira, the berimbau leads the music of the *roda*, the circle of people in which the game is played. Its rhythm sets the pace, and players and singers follow it. An 1835 book of prints by the German artist Johann Moritz Rugendas, Voyage pittoresque dans le Brésil, shows capoeira in Brazil and is one of the best-known early images of the practice.

Brazil's Penal Code of 1890 made capoeira a crime. In the 1930s, Mestre Bimba in Salvador won official registration for his school, and in 1941 Mestre Pastinha founded a center for Capoeira Angola in the same city. In 2008 Brazil's national heritage institute, IPHAN, registered capoeira as cultural heritage. In 2014 UNESCO added the capoeira circle to its list of intangible cultural heritage.

words.d: a musical bow with a wooden rod, a steel wire and a gourd, which leads capoeira music
Portuguese for circle or wheel; the ring of people in which capoeira is played
UNESCO's term for living practices, such as music or ritual, that a community keeps and passes on

look.title: One Bow, Two Records
look.text: Record 1: a berimbau in a museum, its gourd painted and its wooden bow worn smooth near the bottom, labeled Salvador, Bahia, twentieth century. Record 2: the 1890 Brazilian Penal Code, which listed capoeira as a crime.
look.prompt: How does each record tell a different part of capoeira's history? Which one shows the people, and which shows the state?

check.q: What are the three main parts of a berimbau?
choices: a drum, a bell and a stick
a wooden bow, a steel wire and a gourd
a mask, a jacket and a wire
a belt, a sash and a robe
check.why: The berimbau has a verga (bow), an arame (wire) and a cabaça (gourd).

check.q: Which law made capoeira a crime in Brazil?
check.why: Brazil's Penal Code of 1890 criminalized capoeira.

check.q: In what year did UNESCO add the capoeira circle to its intangible heritage list?
check.why: UNESCO inscribed the capoeira circle in 2014; IPHAN registered capoeira in 2008.

lessons.title: Museums, Archives, Halls of Fame
lessons.mainIdea: Museums keep objects, archives keep papers, and halls of fame honor people, and each one chooses what to save.
reading: A museum collects and shows objects. An *archive* keeps records such as letters, minutes of meetings, contracts and photographs. The Olympic Museum in Lausanne, Switzerland, opened in 1993 near the headquarters of the International Olympic Committee. The IOC's Olympic Studies Centre in the same city keeps archives and a library that researchers can use.

A *hall of fame* honors people chosen by a vote. The International Boxing Hall of Fame opened in Canastota, New York, in 1989. Voters, usually boxing writers and historians, choose each year's inductees. A hall of fame is a *selection*, not a full record. Boxers who were never chosen, or who were shut out of big fights, may be missing from its walls.

Every keeper of the past makes choices. A museum may collect only objects that were donated. An archive may keep an association's official minutes but not the letters of people it turned away. A careful researcher asks what each collection left out and looks for other records, such as local newspapers, to fill the gaps.

words.d: a place that keeps records such as letters, minutes, contracts and photographs
an institution that honors people chosen by a vote
a set of items or people that someone chose, which leaves others out

look.title: When Some Keepers Opened
rows: International Boxing Hall of Fame, Canastota
look.cite: Japan Sumo Association; International Boxing Hall of Fame; IOC Olympic Museum records
look.prompt: Which of these three opened first, and how many years before the last?

check.q: What does an archive mainly keep?
choices: records such as letters, minutes and photographs
check.why: An archive holds papers and other records, while a museum shows objects.

check.q: Where is the International Boxing Hall of Fame?
check.why: It opened in Canastota, New York, in 1989.

check.q: Why is a hall of fame called a selection and not a full record?
choices: it lists every boxer who ever fought
voters choose who is honored, so others are left out
it is run by the IOC
check.why: Inductees are chosen by vote, so many people are not included.

review.q: Which of these is a primary source for sumo in the 1800s?
review.why: A banzuke printed at the time is direct evidence from the 1800s.
Provenance is the chain of owners from the maker to today.

review.q: In what year did Kanō Jigorō give the first dan ranks?
review.why: Kanō awarded the first dan ranks at the Kodokan in 1883.

choices: a musical bow that leads capoeira music
review.why: The berimbau is a musical bow with a wire and a gourd that leads the roda.

review.q: Which boxing code first required gloves and three-minute rounds?
review.why: The Queensberry Rules of 1867 required gloves and timed rounds.

review.q: How does a museum caption usually mark a date that is only an estimate?
choices: with a question about the donor
review.why: Circa, written c., means about and marks an estimated date.

review.q: What did the lamé make possible in foil and sabre?
choices: a clear target area for electric scoring
review.why: The metal-thread jacket marks the target area so the scoring box can register touches.

review.q: How are the Olympic Museum and the International Boxing Hall of Fame different?
choices: only the museum honors people chosen by vote
both were founded by the Japan Sumo Association
the hall of fame honors people chosen by vote; the museum shows Olympic objects
review.why: A hall of fame honors voted inductees, while the Olympic Museum shows objects from the Games.

chapters.title: A Plan for Your Own Research
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a researcher build a true account of one martial art from its charters, rule books, admission records and newspapers, and keep legend apart from record?

story.title: Three Papers on a Table
story.kicker: A student spreads out a charter, a rule book and a clipping, and finds that they do not tell the same story.
paragraphs: In a public library near Chicago, a senior named Theo clears a table and lays out three printouts. The first is a translated page about the founding of the Kodokan judo school in Tokyo in 1882. The second is a recent edition of the International Judo Federation's refereeing rules. The third is a scan of an old American newspaper article about a women's judo tournament.

Theo has chosen judo for his research paper. He wants to know when women were allowed to compete at the highest level, and who pushed for it. The founding page says nothing about women. The rule book lists women's weight classes as if they had always been there. Only the newspaper clipping shows that someone had to fight for them.

A librarian stops by and looks at the clipping. She shows Theo how to search the date and the names in a database of digitized newspapers. Within an hour he finds two more articles from other cities about the same event. One spells a name differently. One gives a different number of competitors.

Theo draws a line down a sheet of notebook paper. On the left he writes what the records agree on. On the right he writes what only one record says. At the top he writes his question again, in one sentence, so he will not drift away from it.
story.think: Why might three records about the same martial art disagree, and how should a researcher handle a fact that only one record gives?

lessons.title: One Tradition, One Question
lessons.mainIdea: A strong research paper studies one named tradition and asks one clear question that records can answer.
reading: "Martial arts" is too wide a topic for a short paper. It covers judo, karate, taekwondo, the many Chinese systems, capoeira, fencing, boxing, wrestling, sumo and more. A researcher narrows the topic to one named tradition, and then to one *research question*: a question that can be answered with evidence, such as "When and how did women enter Olympic judo?"

That question can be answered from records. Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi of Brooklyn entered a New York State YMCA judo tournament in 1959 and won her division. Officials took her medal away because she was a woman. She later organized the first Women's World Judo Championships, held at Madison Square Garden in New York in 1980.

At the 1988 Seoul Games, women's judo appeared only as a demonstration, with no official medals. It became a full medal event at the 1992 Barcelona Games. A good research question points straight to records like these: a tournament result, a championship program and Olympic records. A *thesis* is the one-sentence answer the paper argues, and it comes after the evidence is gathered.

words.d: a clear question that can be answered with evidence from records
the one-sentence answer a paper argues, based on its evidence
an Olympic event shown at the Games without official medals

look.title: Wide or Narrow?
look.text: Question A: What is the history of martial arts? Question B: When did the Kodokan open a women's section, and who trained there in its first years? Question C: Why are martial arts popular?
look.prompt: Which question could be answered in a short paper using dated records? Rewrite one of the others so that it could be.

check.q: What happened to Rusty Kanokogi's medal after the 1959 YMCA tournament?
choices: it was placed in a museum
officials took it away because she was a woman
it was given to the Kodokan
it was doubled as a prize
check.why: Kanokogi won her division in 1959, but officials took the medal because she was a woman.

check.q: When did women's judo become a full Olympic medal event?
check.why: It was a demonstration in 1988 and a medal event at Barcelona in 1992.

check.q: What is a thesis?
choices: the one-sentence answer a paper argues
a list of sources at the end
check.why: A thesis is the main claim the paper argues from its evidence.

lessons.title: Finding the Founding Dates
lessons.mainIdea: A tradition can have several founding dates, one for a school, one for a name and one for a governing body, and a researcher records each separately.
reading: A *charter* is a founding document that sets up an organization and states its purpose. Many martial arts have more than one founding moment. Judo dates its school to 1882, when Kanō Jigorō opened the Kodokan in Tokyo. Its world body, the International Judo Federation, was founded in 1951. Those are two different kinds of founding, and a paper should not blur them.

Other arts show the same pattern. The Dai Nippon Butoku Kai, a national body for Japanese martial arts, was founded in Kyoto in 1895. The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913. The International Taekwon-Do Federation was founded in 1966, and the World Taekwondo Federation in 1973. It renamed itself World Taekwondo in 2017.

Karate has a long history in Okinawa, once the Ryukyu Kingdom, before its first world body existed. The World Union of Karate-do Organizations, founded in 1970, later became the World Karate Federation. A researcher builds a simple *chronology*, a list of events in time order, so that the founding of a practice, a name and a body each keep their own date.

words.d: a founding document that sets up an organization and states its purpose
a list of events arranged in the order they happened
the world governing body for judo, founded in 1951

look.title: World Bodies and Their Founding Years
look.cite: Founding records of the FIE, IJF, ITF, WKF and World Taekwondo
look.prompt: Which art had two world bodies founded within seven years of each other?

check.q: What is a charter?
choices: a founding document that sets up an organization
check.why: A charter sets up an organization and states its purpose.

check.q: Why should a judo paper give both 1882 and 1951?
choices: 1882 is the school's founding and 1951 is the world body's
check.why: The Kodokan opened in 1882, and the International Judo Federation was founded in 1951.

check.q: What did the World Taekwondo Federation rename itself in 2017?
check.why: The WTF, founded in 1973, became World Taekwondo in 2017.

lessons.title: Who Governs the Art
lessons.mainIdea: A governing body writes the rules and runs official events, and a researcher names which body governed an art at each date.
reading: A *governing body* writes rules, sets ranks or weight classes, and runs official competitions. At the Olympic level, the International Olympic Committee recognizes one international federation for each sport. That federation writes the rules used at the Games. For judo it is the International Judo Federation, and for fencing it is the FIE.

In the United States, the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 set up a system of *national governing bodies*, one for each Olympic sport, under the United States Olympic Committee. The law was renamed the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act in 1998. USA Judo, USA Fencing and USA Boxing are examples. Each one picks national teams and writes national rules.

Some arts have rival bodies. Taekwondo has two main styles of competition, one tied to the International Taekwon-Do Federation, founded in 1966 by General Choi Hong-hi, and one tied to World Taekwondo and the Kukkiwon, the headquarters in Seoul founded in 1972. Olympic taekwondo follows World Taekwondo rules. A paper names which body it means every time.

words.d: an organization that writes rules and runs official competitions for a sport
in the United States, the group named to run one Olympic sport under the Amateur Sports Act
the World Taekwondo headquarters in Seoul, founded in 1972, which awards dan ranks

look.title: Same Word, Two Bodies
look.text: Two taekwondo certificates hang on a wall. One is signed by the International Taekwon-Do Federation. The other is issued by the Kukkiwon in Seoul. Both use the word taekwondo and both give a dan rank.
look.prompt: Why should a research paper name the body behind each certificate instead of just writing "taekwondo"?

check.q: Which United States law set up national governing bodies for Olympic sports?
check.why: The Amateur Sports Act of 1978 created the national governing body system.

check.q: Which body's rules are used in Olympic taekwondo?
check.why: Olympic taekwondo follows World Taekwondo rules.

check.q: Who founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation in 1966?
check.why: General Choi Hong-hi founded the ITF in 1966.

lessons.title: Editions of a Rule Book
lessons.mainIdea: Rule books change from edition to edition, so a researcher records the year of the edition and compares versions to see what changed.
reading: A governing body reissues its rules when it changes them. Each new printing is an edition, often marked with a year or a version number. The FIE publishes its rules for fencing and updates them after its congress votes on changes. The International Judo Federation also revises its refereeing rules, often in the years between Olympic Games.

Comparing two editions shows what a governing body was worried about. The Queensberry Rules of 1867 differ from the London Prize Ring Rules of 1838 on gloves, rounds and the count after a fall. A researcher who lines up the two codes side by side can list the changes in a table. Each change is a clue to a problem the rule writers wanted to solve.

A *revision* is a change to a published text. Some revisions are small, like a new word. Some are large, like new weight classes or a new scoring system. A research plan lists which editions will be read and where copies are kept, such as the governing body's website, a university *library catalog* or a national library.

words.d: a change made to a published text, such as a rule book
a searchable list of the books and records a library holds
in sports, the formal meeting where members of a federation vote on rules

look.title: Two Editions Side by Side
look.text: London Prize Ring Rules, 1838: bare fists; a round ends when a man goes down. Queensberry Rules, 1867: gloves required; rounds of three minutes with one minute of rest; a fallen boxer has ten seconds to rise.
look.prompt: Make a two-column list of the changes. Which change do you think mattered most for keeping boxing legal, and why?

check.q: What is a revision?
choices: a change made to a published text
check.why: A revision changes the wording or content of a published text like a rule book.

check.q: Why should a paper name the edition of a rule book it used?
check.why: Rules are revised, so a paper must say which version it read.

check.q: Where does a sports federation usually vote on rule changes?
check.why: Federations such as the FIE vote on rule changes at a congress.

lessons.title: Who Was Admitted When
lessons.mainIdea: Admission records show when doors opened to women, to disabled athletes and to others, and each date names a change someone fought for.
reading: The Kodokan opened a formal women's section in 1926. Fukuda Keiko, a granddaughter of one of Kanō Jigorō's own teachers, began training there in 1935. In 2006 the Kodokan promoted her to ninth dan, the first woman to hold that rank. In 2011, USA Judo awarded her a tenth dan. She taught for decades in San Francisco.

Olympic records give clear dates for women. Women's foil fencing entered the Olympics in 1924 in Paris. Women's judo became a medal event in 1992, women's taekwondo in 2000, women's freestyle wrestling in 2004 and women's boxing in 2012. In Illinois, the IHSA held its first girls wrestling state finals in 2022. *Title IX* of the Education Amendments of 1972 bans sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money.

Disability is part of the record too. Judo joined the *Paralympic Games* in 1988 in Seoul, for blind and visually impaired athletes. Women's Paralympic judo followed in 2004 in Athens. A research plan lists each door, the date it opened, and the record that proves it, such as an Olympic results book, a Paralympic record or a law.

words.d: part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in schools receiving federal money
the international games for athletes with disabilities; judo joined in 1988
judo teacher who began at the Kodokan in 1935 and became its first woman ninth dan in 2006

look.title: Women's First Olympic Medal Events
look.unit: year of first women's medal event
look.cite: IOC Olympic results records, Paris 1924 to London 2012
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first women's fencing event and the first women's boxing event?

check.q: When did the Kodokan open a formal women's section?
check.why: The Kodokan opened its women's section in 1926.

check.q: In which year did women's boxing enter the Olympics?
check.why: Women's boxing became an Olympic medal event at London in 2012.

check.q: When did judo join the Paralympic Games?
check.why: Judo for blind and visually impaired athletes joined the Paralympics in Seoul in 1988.

lessons.title: Rooms That Were Closed
lessons.mainIdea: Records of exclusion, such as boxing's color line and Brazil's ban on capoeira, are part of a tradition's history and need dated evidence.
reading: In American boxing in the late 1800s, a *color line* kept Black boxers from fighting for the world heavyweight title. Champion John L. Sullivan publicly refused to fight Black challengers. On December 26, 1908, in Sydney, Australia, Jack Johnson defeated Tommy Burns and became the first Black world heavyweight champion. Many white newspapers and promoters then called for a "great white hope" to beat him.

Law closed rooms as well. Brazil's Penal Code of 1890 made capoeira a crime, and police records from Rio de Janeiro and Salvador list arrests for it. In the 1930s, under President Getúlio Vargas, the government began to permit capoeira in registered schools. Mestre Bimba's school in Salvador won official registration in 1937.

An *exclusion* is a rule or custom that keeps a group out. A paper that leaves exclusion out tells only part of the story. A researcher looks for the rule or custom, the date it began, the date it ended, and the people who pushed against it. *Primary evidence* for these changes includes court and police records, newspaper reports and laws.

words.d: a rule or custom that kept Black athletes out of certain competitions
a rule or custom that keeps a group of people out
American boxer who became the first Black world heavyweight champion in 1908
records made at the time, such as laws, police files and newspaper reports

look.title: Reading a Silence
look.text: A list of heavyweight champions from the 1880s and 1890s shows only white boxers. A newspaper from the same years quotes the champion saying he will not fight a Black challenger. A later record shows Jack Johnson winning the title in Sydney in 1908.
look.prompt: What does the champions list leave out? How do the other two records change the way you read it?

check.q: Who became the first Black world heavyweight champion in 1908?
check.why: Jack Johnson defeated Tommy Burns in Sydney on December 26, 1908.

check.q: What is a color line?
choices: a rule or custom that kept Black athletes out
a painted boundary on a mat
check.why: The color line barred Black boxers from title fights.

check.q: When did Mestre Bimba's school win official registration?
check.why: Bimba's school in Salvador was registered in 1937, after capoeira had been banned in 1890.

lessons.title: The Shaolin Legend
lessons.mainIdea: A popular legend links Shaolin fighting arts to the monk Bodhidharma, but historians trace that link to a text from the 1600s.
reading: The Shaolin Monastery stands on Mount Song in Henan Province, China. A famous *legend* says that the Indian monk Bodhidharma came to Shaolin around the 500s and taught the monks exercises that grew into fighting arts. The story appears in many martial arts books, films and school histories around the world.

Historians have tested the legend against records. A stone *stele* at Shaolin, dated 728, records that monks helped the future Tang emperor Li Shimin in a war in the 620s. That is real evidence of fighting monks. But the earliest known text linking Bodhidharma to fighting exercises is a preface to the Yijin Jing, the Muscle Change Classic, dated 1624. Historians regard that preface as a later invention.

In the 1930s, the Chinese historian Tang Hao questioned the Bodhidharma story in his studies of martial arts. The historian Meir Shahar examined the evidence in The Shaolin Monastery, published in 2008. A careful paper tells the legend, labels it as a legend, and sets it beside what the stele and other records can prove. Shaolin is also only one of the many Chinese martial arts traditions.

words.d: a traditional story told as history that cannot be proven by records
an upright stone slab carved with words, often to record an event
an Indian Buddhist monk whom a legend links to Shaolin fighting arts

look.title: Stone and Story
look.text: Record: a stele at Shaolin, dated 728, says monks aided Li Shimin in the 620s. Story: a preface dated 1624 says Bodhidharma taught the monks exercises in the 500s. The two texts are about 900 years apart.
look.prompt: Which text is closer in time to the events it describes? How should a paper use each one?

check.q: What does the Shaolin stele dated 728 record?
choices: monks helping the future emperor Li Shimin
check.why: The stele records that Shaolin monks aided Li Shimin in the 620s.

check.q: What is the earliest known text linking Bodhidharma to fighting exercises?
choices: a preface to the Yijin Jing dated 1624
check.why: The Yijin Jing preface of 1624 is the earliest known source for the link, and historians see it as a later invention.

check.q: Who wrote The Shaolin Monastery, published in 2008?
check.why: Meir Shahar's 2008 book examines the Shaolin evidence.

lessons.title: Stories Told About Capoeira
lessons.mainIdea: A popular story says capoeira was disguised as a dance, and historians weigh it against police records, laws and images from the 1800s.
reading: A story often told about *capoeira* says that enslaved Africans in Brazil hid a fighting art inside a dance so that slaveholders would not notice. The story is repeated in many schools and books. Historians say that no documents from the time of slavery confirm it. They treat it as a story that expresses pride and resistance rather than a proven fact.

The records that do exist tell a detailed story. Police files from Rio de Janeiro in the early 1800s record arrests of enslaved and free Black men for capoeira. Rugendas's prints of 1835 show it being played to a drum. The Penal Code of 1890 made it a crime across Brazil, two years after slavery was abolished by the Golden Law of 1888.

The historian Matthias Röhrig Assunção studied these records in Capoeira: The History of an Afro-Brazilian Martial Art, published in 2005. A researcher can respect the story as part of how capoeira communities remember their past, while writing clearly that the documented history comes from police files, laws and images. *Corroboration* means checking a claim against a second, independent record.

words.d: an Afro-Brazilian martial art played in a circle to music
support for a claim from a second, independent record
the Brazilian law of 1888 that abolished slavery

look.title: Story and File
look.text: Story: capoeira was hidden inside a dance so slaveholders would not notice it. File: a police register from Rio de Janeiro in the early 1800s lists the arrest of a man for capoeira in a public square.
look.prompt: Does the police file support the story, challenge it, or do neither? Explain what each source can and cannot show.

check.q: What do historians say about the story that capoeira was disguised as a dance?
choices: no documents from the time of slavery confirm it
the Penal Code of 1890 proves it
check.why: Historians have found no records from the slavery era that confirm the disguise story.

check.q: What law abolished slavery in Brazil in 1888?
check.why: The Golden Law of 1888 ended slavery in Brazil.

check.q: What does corroboration mean?
choices: support for a claim from a second, independent record
check.why: Corroboration means a second, independent record backs up the claim.

lessons.title: Weighing a Newspaper Clipping
lessons.mainIdea: A newspaper report is a primary source written fast and for readers, so a researcher checks it against other papers and official records.
reading: Newspapers reported martial arts and combat sports for well over a century. When James J. Corbett beat John L. Sullivan in New Orleans in 1892, papers across the country printed long accounts. When Jack Johnson won the title in 1908, reports differed sharply by who owned the paper and who read it. A news report shows what was known, and what was believed, on a certain day.

The Library of Congress runs *Chronicling America*, a free online collection of digitized historic American newspapers, launched in 2007 with the National Endowment for the Humanities. Researchers can search it by name, date and state. Many public libraries also give card holders access to digitized archives of large papers such as the Chicago Tribune.

A clipping can be wrong. Reporters wrote on deadline, spelled foreign names in many ways and sometimes printed rumors. Papers also had points of view, called *bias*. A researcher compares at least two papers, then checks their claims against records such as official results, rule books or charters. A fact reported by only one paper is marked as uncertain in the notes.

words.d: a free Library of Congress website of digitized historic American newspapers, launched in 2007
a point of view that shapes how a source tells a story
an article cut or copied from a newspaper

look.title: Two Reports, One Night
look.text: Paper 1 says the crowd at a boxing match was about 10,000 and praises the winner. Paper 2, from another city, says the crowd was about 6,000 and spends most of its story on the betting. The official promoter's record is lost.
look.prompt: How would you write the crowd size in your paper? What other record could you search for?

check.q: What is Chronicling America?
choices: a Library of Congress collection of digitized historic newspapers
check.why: Chronicling America is a free Library of Congress newspaper collection launched in 2007.

check.q: What should a researcher do with a fact reported by only one paper?
check.why: A single report is not corroborated, so it should be marked uncertain.

check.q: What is bias in a source?
choices: the date a paper was printed
a point of view that shapes how a story is told
check.why: Bias is a point of view that shapes what a source says and leaves out.

lessons.title: Citing Each Institution
lessons.mainIdea: A citation tells readers exactly where a fact came from, and a governing body or museum can be cited as the author of its own records.
reading: A *citation* names the source of a fact so a reader can find it. The Chicago Manual of Style, first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906, is one of the most widely used guides for citing sources in history. The MLA Handbook, from the Modern Language Association, is another common guide in schools.

Organizations can be authors. A rule book is cited under the governing body that wrote it, such as the International Judo Federation or the FIE, with the title, edition year and where it was found. A museum object is cited by the museum's name, the object's title, its date and its accession number. A law is cited by its name and year, such as the Amateur Sports Act of 1978.

Books are cited by author, title, publisher and year. For example, a paper on Shaolin might cite Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery: History, Religion, and the Chinese Martial Arts, University of Hawai'i Press, 2008. A *bibliography* lists every source at the end of a paper. Keeping it while researching, not after, saves hours of searching.

words.d: a note that names the source of a fact so a reader can find it
a list of every source used, placed at the end of a paper
a guide to writing and citing sources, first published by the University of Chicago Press in 1906

look.title: Fix the Citation
look.text: A student's note says only: "judo rules, internet." The student used the International Judo Federation's refereeing rules, found on the federation's website, in an edition dated with a year on the cover.
look.prompt: Rewrite the note as a full citation. What three facts did the first note leave out?

check.q: Who first published the Chicago Manual of Style in 1906?
check.why: The University of Chicago Press first published the guide in 1906.

check.q: How is a rule book usually cited?
choices: under the governing body that wrote it, with title and edition year
under the name of the reader
under the name of the gym that owns a copy
check.why: A governing body is the author of its rule book, and the edition year matters.

check.q: What is a bibliography?
choices: a list of every source used, at the end of a paper
check.why: A bibliography lists all the sources a paper used.

lessons.title: Shaping a Short Paper
lessons.mainIdea: A short research paper moves from a question to a thesis, supports it with dated records, answers the strongest counterevidence and ends with what remains unknown.
reading: A short paper has a clear shape. It opens with the research question and the thesis. Its body gives the evidence in time order or by theme, with a citation for each fact. It then answers *counterevidence*, the records that seem to point the other way. It ends by naming what the records still do not show.

Take karate as a case. Karate grew in Okinawa, once the Ryukyu Kingdom, and was brought to mainland Japan in the 1920s. Funakoshi Gichin demonstrated it in Tokyo in 1922. Karate made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo 2020 Games, held in 2021 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. It was not included in the Paris 2024 program.

A thesis about that case might argue that Olympic entry depended on host-city choices as much as on how widely karate was practiced. The paper would cite the IOC's program decisions and World Karate Federation records. Counterevidence might include the size of karate's worldwide membership. A plan that lists each claim beside its record shows gaps before writing begins.

words.d: records that seem to point against a paper's thesis
Okinawan teacher who demonstrated karate in Tokyo in 1922
the island kingdom, centered on Okinawa, where karate first developed

look.title: Olympic Debut Years

look.prompt: Which two arts entered the Olympics in the same year? Which entered last?

check.q: What is counterevidence?
choices: records that seem to point against the thesis
check.why: Counterevidence is evidence a paper must answer because it seems to cut against the thesis.

check.q: When did karate make its Olympic debut?
choices: at the Tokyo 2020 Games, held in 2021
check.why: Karate debuted at Tokyo 2020, held in 2021, and was not in the Paris 2024 program.

check.q: Where did karate first develop?
choices: in Okinawa, once the Ryukyu Kingdom
check.why: Karate grew in Okinawa, the center of the old Ryukyu Kingdom, before reaching mainland Japan.

choices: a question that can be answered with evidence from records
review.why: A research question points to records that can answer it.

review.q: In what year was the International Judo Federation founded?
review.why: The IJF was founded in 1951; the Kodokan dates to 1882.

review.q: What does Title IX of 1972 ban?
choices: sex discrimination in schools receiving federal money
review.why: Title IX bans sex discrimination in schools that receive federal funds.

review.q: How do historians treat the story that Bodhidharma taught fighting arts at Shaolin?
choices: as written in the Queensberry Rules
as a legend traced to a text of 1624
review.why: The earliest link is the 1624 Yijin Jing preface, which historians regard as a later invention.

review.q: What should a researcher do before trusting a newspaper claim?
choices: check it against a second paper and official records
review.why: Corroboration with other papers and records tests a claim.

review.q: Which United States law created national governing bodies for Olympic sports?
review.why: The Amateur Sports Act of 1978 set up national governing bodies.

review.q: How do the ITF and World Taekwondo differ?
choices: they are rival taekwondo bodies, and Olympic taekwondo uses World Taekwondo rules
review.why: Both govern taekwondo; the Olympics follow World Taekwondo rules.

choices: a list of every source used
review.why: A bibliography lists all of a paper's sources at the end.
